segments.text: Most teams don't realize their database is the slowest part of their app.
I see it all the time when I'm reviewing code.
The page loads, the API is fast, and then one query takes two full seconds.
So why does that happen?
Usually it's a missing index on a column you filter by every single request.
Think of an index like the table of contents in a book.
Without it, the database reads every page to find one line.
With it, it jumps straight to the right page.
Here's the biggest mistake I made early in my career.
I added indexes to everything because I thought more was always better.
Every index makes reads faster but writes slower.
Our insert times doubled and nobody knew why for a week.
The fix was simple once we measured it.
We dropped eleven indexes nobody was using.
Writes got fast again and reads didn't change at all.
So here's the rule I follow now.
Measure first, then index the queries that actually run the most.
How do you know which queries those are?
Turn on query insights and sort by total time, not average time.
A query that takes ten milliseconds but runs a million times matters more than one slow report.
That one change saved us real money on our cloud bill.
The second thing is connection limits.
When traffic spikes, every serverless function opens its own connection.
Your database runs out of connections long before it runs out of CPU.
Connection pooling fixes that by sharing a small number of connections.
It's the difference between a launch day that works and one that falls over.
If you take one thing away from this talk, make it this.
Your database is part of your product experience.
Treat it that way and your users will feel the difference.
Thanks for having me.
